options.claimRepresented: Publish is the action for a nonexecuting approval artifact.
options.whyIncorrectInContext: Publish carries out a deployment rather than stopping at the requested T-SQL review artifact. A no-op publish still does not make Publish the specified artifact-generation action.
options.couldBeCorrectWhen: The proposed changes have already been approved and the job is authorized to apply the package to the target, rather than merely submit its SQL for approval.
options.evidenceSummary: The build unit's Deploy the project section uses Publish for new or existing database updates; both units separately prescribe Script for nonexecuting T-SQL review. No universal drop behavior is assumed.

options.claimRepresented: Script generates the proposed source-to-target deployment T-SQL.
options.whyIncorrectInContext: Supported, not incorrect: the requested deliverable is executable-format T-SQL and deployment must not be applied. Script is the documented action satisfying both requirements.
options.couldBeCorrectWhen: A valid source package and readable target schema are available and the artifact will be reviewed before execution. If the target or publish settings subsequently change, the plan needs renewed review.
options.evidenceSummary: Generate a deployment script explicitly says Script produces the T-SQL without running it and recommends retaining Deployment.sql as a pipeline approval artifact.

options.claimRepresented: DeployReport returns the actual deployment T-SQL artifact.
options.whyIncorrectInContext: It returns an XML operations summary rather than the actual T-SQL. It is nonexecuting and useful for approval, but fails the explicit output-format requirement.
options.couldBeCorrectWhen: An approver or automated policy needs a machine-readable list of planned operations or high-impact changes instead of the complete deployment SQL.
options.evidenceSummary: Both read units distinguish Script's SQL from DeployReport's XML; the drift unit gives operation and alert examples rather than a runnable SQL payload.

options.claimRepresented: Extract computes this built package's proposed deployment SQL.
options.whyIncorrectInContext: Extract reads a database schema into a model or object files. Producing SQL object-definition files does not make it a source-package-to-target deployment script.
options.couldBeCorrectWhen: The task is to baseline the live schema, import approved database changes, or obtain source-controlled object definitions for a separate comparison.
options.evidenceSummary: Automate with SqlPackage extract uses a SourceConnectionString and SchemaObjectType output. The later Script section separately compares the built source model with the target.

sourceSummaries.dp800-d2-reference-data: The actual reference-data unit places seeding after schema deployment, notes post scripts run every deployment, and contrasts plain INSERT replay with matched/not-matched reconciliation. The duplicate-key warning is about plain inserts, not the INSERT verb in every possible data script. That qualification matters because option B does not expressly say unconditional replay.

options.claimRepresented: Seed the newly modeled lookup table before the schema plan executes.
options.whyIncorrectInContext: The first deployment creates the lookup table in the schema plan, so it is not yet available at the proposed seeding time. Later-run success cannot satisfy the initial deployment requirement.
options.couldBeCorrectWhen: The needed table already exists before this deployment and the data preparation must precede compatible schema changes. A script that independently creates the table would be a different, unstated workflow.
options.evidenceSummary: The source distinguishes preparation before the plan from post-plan lookup population. The candidate explicitly assigns initial table creation to the plan, ruling out this timing.

options.claimRepresented: Append reference rows using INSERT after the schema deployment.
options.whyIncorrectInContext: A blind replay of the same primary keys is incorrect, but that restriction is absent from B. An append operation guarded to insert only missing keys remains an INSERT-based post-schema strategy. With unchanged reference values, that reading can satisfy the stated presence and rerun requirements.
options.couldBeCorrectWhen: The required values do not change, each execution skips already present stable keys, and only missing rows are inserted after table creation. The stem does not require updating changed values, and the option does not explicitly prohibit such a guard. No particular SQL syntax or concurrency implementation is asserted.
options.evidenceSummary: Write idempotent reference data scripts limits its failure warning to plain INSERT replay and demonstrates separating existing from missing keys. The authored distractor explanation adds 'without handling existing rows', which the option itself never states. This is an unexcluded contextual interpretation, not an executed counterexample.

options.claimRepresented: Use a versioned post-deployment reconciliation script for existing and missing keys.
options.whyIncorrectInContext: Supported, not incorrect: post-plan execution gives the new table time to exist, and explicit existing/missing-key reconciliation addresses reruns. The hold concerns exclusivity against B, not C's technical soundness.
options.couldBeCorrectWhen: The script correctly implements the reference-data policy after schema creation and handles already-present keys. Correct deletion policy, changed values and concurrent writers would need separate implementation decisions if introduced.
options.evidenceSummary: The source describes versioning data scripts alongside schema and illustrates post-deployment matched/not-matched handling. It does not say every implementation using a different DML form is invalid.

options.claimRepresented: The schema model alone supplies the required reference rows.
options.whyIncorrectInContext: The question assigns row population to this deployment lifecycle and the declarative model supplies schema objects, not those required data values. Merely creating the table leaves the stated row requirement unmet.
options.couldBeCorrectWhen: No lookup rows are required, or a separately specified authorized data-provisioning process supplies them after schema deployment. No such process is given here.
options.evidenceSummary: The unit explicitly introduces pre/post data scripts because essential lookup and configuration rows sit outside the compiled schema model.

challenges.plan: No service pricing plan or IDE feature changes the ordering problem. The critical distinction is the data script's conditions, not a vendor plan or a mandatory MERGE implementation.
challenges.role: No particular permission level is tested. Any real data script needs authorized data access; granting higher privilege would not cure blind key duplication or missing-table timing.
challenges.preconditions: The initial absence and later retention of the table are sufficient to choose post-plan timing. They are insufficient to exclude guarded insertion: existing values are not said to change, and B does not specify unconditional inserts.
challenges.featureStatus: SDK-style post-deployment scripts and SQL primary-key/data operations are real GA claims. They cannot be labeled Not applicable merely because the item asks for a strategy. No preview IDE is needed.

challenges.stemSufficiency: HOLD: C is sound, but B can describe a post-schema append that skips existing stable keys when values remain unchanged. Neither the option nor stem excludes that interpretation. The distractor explanation supplies the missing 'without handling existing' premise afterward.
challenges.explanationBounds: The C explanation is supported. B's categorical exclusion depends on an unspoken implementation, and the deep explanation's 'only' claim is therefore too strong. MERGE syntax or universal concurrency safety is not required or approved.
challenges.reasoningDepth: Initial ordering plus repeated-key state is genuine Intermediate implementation reasoning. Difficulty is not the defect; the breadth of INSERT wording prevents a unique single-select key.
challenges.answerClues: C states both desired properties explicitly and is more comprehensive than the alternatives. That can lead readers to the intended answer without resolving B's semantic breadth. The absence of lexical warnings does not prove unique correctness.

It describes execution on each deployment, not automatic cleanup of test-owned rows. A green model build therefore supplies no data-reset guarantee for this scenario.

options.claimRepresented: A fixed successful execution order makes the unit tests independent.
options.whyIncorrectInContext: A favorable order hides the residual-row dependency; it does not make shuffled independent tests start from the intended state.

options.whyIncorrectInContext: Supported, not incorrect: deterministic setup removes dependency on predecessor state while owned-data cleanup prevents later contamination, without discarding total assertions.
options.couldBeCorrectWhen: Setup and cleanup manage the rows relevant to each test on the dedicated target. Parallel execution would additionally require isolation of concurrent test ownership; the stem only describes shuffled order.
options.evidenceSummary: The documented test structure explicitly inserts/clears data in pre-test actions and cleans up in post-test actions, with known-state requirements for both unit and integration tests.

options.whyIncorrectInContext: Build validation checks the model, not live test-data cleanup. Even deployment-script behavior is outside that model validation, and the stem expressly says this redeployment retains the rows.
options.couldBeCorrectWhen: A separately configured and tested reset process runs as part of test preparation. In that different workflow, cleanup belongs to the reset process, never to the bare model build claimed by D.
options.evidenceSummary: Testing guidance distinguishes structure from behavior, and the pre/post product article excludes script execution correctness from compilation. Neither gives model build an automatic data-deletion side effect.

sourceSummaries.dp800-d2x-pre-post-deployment: The product article directly explains that Build Remove excludes a child script but removes it from the VS Code project view, while adding it as None restores visibility. It also states Microsoft.Build.Sql combines SQLCMD children into the single packaged pre/post script, which is not model-compiled.

options.claimRepresented: Build Remove excludes the referenced seed file from model compilation.
options.whyIncorrectInContext: Supported, not incorrect as part of the required pair: the data-changing child script must not be treated as a schema definition under default SQL globbing.
options.couldBeCorrectWhen: The removed file remains reachable through the valid PostDeploy SQLCMD include, and None Include separately restores the requested VS Code project visibility. Removing a required table definition would be a different and harmful use.

options.claimRepresented: Deleting the authored seed source while retaining its include meets the requirements.
options.whyIncorrectInContext: It breaks the retained include and removes the required versioned data logic. Excluding compilation is not deleting the file or its source history.
options.couldBeCorrectWhen: A no-longer-needed authored script is deliberately retired with its references updated, or a disposable generated file is ignored. The named seed and unchanged include in this option do not meet those conditions.
options.evidenceSummary: Reference data belongs in source control; the sources prescribe item classification, not deleting SQLCMD-referenced authored data scripts.

options.claimRepresented: None Include keeps the Build-removed seed visible in the VS Code project.
options.whyIncorrectInContext: Supported, not incorrect as the companion to A: the file must be visible while excluded from the compiled database model. None alone is not being claimed to cancel Build globbing.
options.couldBeCorrectWhen: Build Remove has also been applied and the child remains included by the single PostDeploy entry point. Without the SQLCMD include, None by itself would not schedule data execution.
options.evidenceSummary: The product article explicitly re-adds Build-removed SQL files as None to restore VS Code visibility, while preserving model exclusion.

options.claimRepresented: The same SQL project may add a second independent PostDeploy entry point.
options.whyIncorrectInContext: The documented project contract permits one post-deployment entry point. Multiple files belong behind that entry point through includes, as already configured.
options.couldBeCorrectWhen: The file becomes the sole post-deployment entry point of a different project, or replaces the existing one with references reorganized. It cannot be an additional independent entry point in this same project.
options.evidenceSummary: Both sources state the single pre/single post limit and show SQLCMD :r combining multiple files into the permitted entry point.
